findings.description: The inline policy grants wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", violating least privilege. Because the same user holds a long-lived static access key, theft of that key yields full control of compute, storage, and serverless resources in the account, enabling S3 data exfiltration and privilege escalation via ec2:RunInstances / lambda with instance or execution roles.

A static IAM access key is minted for a service identity instead of using an assumable role with short-lived STS credentials. The key does not expire or rotate, and it is bound to an identity holding wildcard permissions, making it a durable high-value credential-theft target.

No pgp_key is supplied, so the secret access key is written in cleartext to the Terraform state file (the encrypted_secret attribute is only populated when a PGP key is given). Anyone with read access to state obtains working credentials for this over-privileged user.

The root module output svc_deploy_key_material exports access key secret material and is not marked sensitive = true, so the value can be rendered in CLI/plan output, CI/CD logs, and read by any consumer of the remote state.

findings.issue_category: privileged IAM user without permissions boundary
findings.description: A persistent programmatic IAM user carries admin-like inline permissions with no permissions boundary and no conditional constraints (MFA, source IP, or aws:PrincipalOrgID), so there is no defence-in-depth limit on the wildcard grant if the static key is compromised. An assumable role with a boundary would be the safer pattern.
